<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="nuclear-basics" data-src="../assets/learn/data/f05-nuclear-basics.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The idea in one table: hold the chain reaction steady (an illustrative toy)</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f5-fbt">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Control rods in</th><th scope="col">Moderator left</th><th scope="col">Each split leads to (k)</th><th scope="col">100 neutrons after 12 generations</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>0%</td><td>100%</td><td>1.25 more splits: growing</td><td>1,455</td></tr>
<tr><td>40%</td><td>100%</td><td>1.00: steady (critical)</td><td>100</td></tr>
<tr><td>40%</td><td>40%</td><td>0.64: dying out</td><td>under one</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">From fuel to steam: the two U.S. plant types</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f5-fbt">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Type</th><th scope="col">Vessel pressure (<span class="lx-term" data-term="megapascal">MPa</span>, megapascals)</th><th scope="col">Water temperature</th><th scope="col">Where the steam forms</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Pressurized water (PWR)</td><td>about 15 MPa</td><td>about 326 °C</td><td>in a steam generator, in a second loop</td></tr>
<tr><td>Boiling water (BWR)</td><td>about 7 MPa</td><td>about 288 °C</td><td>in the vessel itself</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
<p>Prairie Town's 100 MW plant (illustrative), at the 32.7% efficiency implied by EIA's 2025 tested heat rate: its core makes about 306 MW of heat. About 206 MW is rejected heat and other losses, mostly through the condenser.</p>
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Designs compared by size, outlet temperature and uses</p>
<div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f5-fbt wide">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Design</th><th scope="col">Size</th><th scope="col">Coolant</th><th scope="col">Outlet temperature</th><th scope="col">Uses</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>Large water-cooled</td><td>1,000 MWe or higher</td><td>ordinary water</td><td>about 300 °C</td><td>electricity; some district heating and desalination</td></tr>
<tr><td>Small water-cooled</td><td>300 MWe or less</td><td>ordinary water</td><td>about 300 °C</td><td>electricity; some district heating and desalination</td></tr>
<tr><td>Microreactor</td><td>1 to 20 MWt</td><td>gas, liquid metal, molten salt, or a fluid inside heat pipes</td><td>depends on the coolant</td><td>heat used directly, or electricity</td></tr>
<tr><td>Sodium-cooled fast</td><td>varies</td><td>liquid sodium, at low pressure</td><td>about 500 to 550 °C</td><td>electricity</td></tr>
<tr><td>High-temperature gas-cooled</td><td>up to 600 MWt per module, for passive cooling</td><td>helium</td><td>700 to 950 °C</td><td>electricity; industrial heat at 650 to 950 °C, hydrogen production among it</td></tr>
<tr><td>Salt-cooled high-temperature (concept)</td><td>varies</td><td>molten fluoride salt, at low pressure</td><td>700 to 950 °C</td><td>electricity or industrial heat</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table></div>
<p>A design's outlet temperature can overlap a heat use's band, but overlap is not capability: heat flows only from hotter to cooler, through heat exchangers, and the chosen design decides.</p>
<p><b>After shutdown:</b> the control rods stop the chain reaction, but the fission products keep giving off decay heat, so cooling must go on.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you work through this step by step: fire a neutron, steady a chain reaction, open a plant, sort its parts, guess its heat and line designs up against heat uses.</p>
</div>

<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Real numbers, designs.</b> Pressures, temperatures, sizes and heat uses: U.S. Department of Energy, <a href="https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2016/01/f28/QTR2015-4M-Light-Water-Reactors.pdf">Quadrennial Technology Review 2015</a> and its companion assessments (2015), read 3 November 2026.</span></p>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Real numbers, efficiency.</b> EIA's 2025 <a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_08_01.html">tested heat rate for nuclear units</a>, 10,443 <span class="lx-term" data-term="btu">Btu</span> (British thermal units, a unit of heat) per kWh, against 3,412 Btu in a kWh; read 3 November 2026.</span></p>

## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f5-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Fission</dt><dd>A neutron splits a uranium-235 nucleus into two smaller atoms, a few new neutrons and heat.</dd>
<dt>A steady chain</dt><dd>Control rods absorb neutrons and a moderator slows them; a reactor is held so each split leads to exactly one more (critical, k = 1).</dd>
<dt>Fuel to steam</dt><dd>A pressurized-water plant keeps its core water liquid at about 15 MPa and boils a second loop; a boiling-water plant boils in the vessel at about 7 MPa.</dd>
<dt>A heat source first</dt><dd>At the 32.7% efficiency implied by EIA's 2025 tested heat rate, Prairie Town's 100 MW plant makes about 306 MW of heat; about 206 MW is rejected heat and losses, mostly through the condenser.</dd>
<dt>After shutdown</dt><dd>Stopping the chain reaction does not stop decay heat from the fission products, so cooling must go on.</dd>
<dt>Temperature limits the uses</dt><dd>Water-cooled designs reach about 300 °C; high-temperature designs reach 700 to 950 °C, which overlaps the 650 to 950 °C band many industrial processes need. Overlap is not capability: the design and its heat exchangers decide.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>What lets a chain reaction be held steady</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Delayed neutrons.** A small share of the neutrons from fission come out seconds late, from decaying fission products. They slow the chain's response enough for control rods to keep pace (DOE Fundamentals Handbook, 1993).
- **One water, two jobs.** In U.S. plants the water around the fuel is both the coolant and the moderator (DOE, 2025). In the toy, less moderator means a smaller k: less water, less slowing.
- **No moderator at all.** Sodium-cooled fast designs avoid slowing their neutrons, using coolants made of heavier atoms; water's hydrogen is what slows neutrons in today's plants (DOE, 2015).
- **Richer fuel.** Most microreactor designs need fuel with more uranium-235 than today's 3% to 5%; some may need less by using high-temperature moderators (DOE, 2021). One such fuel, HALEU, holds 5% to less than 20% (DOE, 2024).
- **Hotter heat, higher efficiency.** EIA's 2025 tested heat rate for U.S. nuclear units implies about 32.7%. DOE puts a high-temperature design at about 47% at 850 °C: the heat-engine idea of [F4](f04-power-plants.qmd).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>How the toy works, and a plant as a model sees it</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

**The toy.** Each generation holds $k$ times the neutrons of the one before. Pushing the rods in lowers $k$, and so does draining the moderator; the toy's values show the idea and are not taken from a real core.

Steady means exactly $k = 1$: here only with the moderator full and the rods 40% in (rods 30%, moderator 90% gives $k = 0.999$, a slow decline). Real cores are modeled with neutron transport and kinetics, a field of its own (side topic [X1](x01-under-the-hood.html)).

**A plant in a system model.** Grid models such as [lesson 6](06-three-jobs.qmd), [M2](m02-unit-commitment.qmd) and [lesson 13](13-capstone.qmd) take a plant as a few numbers: its size in MW, its [heat rate]{.lx-term term="heat-rate"} or efficiency, its [capacity factor]{.lx-term term="capacity-factor"} and its [refuelling outages]{.lx-term term="refuelling-outage"}. The U.S. fleet's capacity factor was 91.1% in 2025 (EIA, Table 6.07.B; [lesson 5](05-capacity-factor.qmd)).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Neutron physics beyond the toy: the many fission products, cross sections and the kinetics of a real core (side topic <a href="x01-under-the-hood.html">X1</a>).</li>
<li>Radiation, shielding and health effects.</li>
<li>The fuel cycle before the fuel arrives: mining, conversion and enrichment of uranium.</li>
<li>The final disposal of spent fuel.</li>
<li>Accident analysis and safety regulation.</li>
<li>Each advanced design's details beyond its size, coolant, outlet temperature and uses.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

::: {#check .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 5 minutes: five myths, then two questions.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f5-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="liquid" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Spent nuclear fuel is a glowing green liquid.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It goes in and comes out solid: ceramic pellets in sealed metal rods (DOE, 2022). Being highly radioactive, it is kept under water, later in steel and concrete casks.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="space" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “All the spent fuel from U.S. commercial plants since the 1950s would cover a city.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. DOE estimated in October 2022 that all 90,000 metric tons would cover one football field, less than 10 yards deep. That is the fuel alone, without a storage site's spacing and buildings.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="energyleft" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Fuel taken out after five years has used up nearly all of its energy.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. More than 90% of its potential energy is still there (DOE, 2022). Recycling can turn part of the used fuel into new fuel; as of 2022, France recycles and the United States does not.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="boil" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “In a pressurized-water plant, the water in the core boils.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. At about 15 MPa it stays liquid at about 326 °C; the steam forms in a second loop, in the steam generator (DOE, 2015). Boiling-water plants do boil in the vessel.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="passive" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Every safety system needs pumps, power or an operator to work.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. <span class="lx-term" data-term="passive-safety">Passive systems</span> use natural effects, like hot coolant rising and cool coolant sinking, to keep fuel cool (DOE, 2015). U.S. plants today rely mainly on active ones; newer water-cooled designs typically add passive ones.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f5">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="eff" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">A core makes 600 MW of heat. At 32.7% <span class="lx-term" data-term="efficiency">efficiency</span>, the figure implied by EIA's 2025 tested heat rate, about how much electricity does the plant send out?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">196 MW</li><li data-value="b">600 MW</li><li data-value="c">404 MW</li><li data-value="d">33 MW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>196 MW: 600 × 0.327. The other 404 MW is rejected heat and other losses, mostly low-temperature heat through the condenser.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="soec" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A solid-oxide <span class="lx-term" data-term="electrolyzer">electrolyzer</span> runs at 650 to 850 °C, where heat can do part of the work of splitting water. Which design's <span class="lx-term" data-term="outlet-temperature">outlet temperature</span> overlaps that band?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Large water-cooled, about 300 °C</li><li data-value="b">Sodium-cooled fast, about 500 to 550 °C</li><li data-value="c">High-temperature gas-cooled, 700 to 950 °C</li><li data-value="d">None of them</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>High-temperature gas-cooled: its 700 to 950 °C outlet overlaps the band (DOE). A real plant also needs a hot enough design and heat exchangers. The other two stay below 650 °C.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<ol>
<li><b>Two types:</b> every U.S. power plant of this kind is water-cooled; more than 65% are pressurized-water and roughly a third boiling-water plants (DOE, 2025).</li>
<li><b>Fuel:</b> pellets are stacked in sealed rods about 1 cm wide, bundled into assemblies; how many rods and assemblies a core holds depends on its design and power (EIA; DOE).</li>
<li><b>Heat beyond electricity:</b> some water-cooled plants already supply district heat or desalinated water (DOE, 2015).</li>
</ol>
</div>
